groups.title: Backup & Recovery
groups.question: Explain how you would back up a production database and prove you can restore it.

followUps.pg_dump, pg_basebackup & Point-in-Time R: Why isn't a nightly pg_dump enough for a busy production database, and what does point-in-time recovery add?
followUps.Testing Restores — The Missing Step: Why should you test restores regularly, and what would you check after one?

evidence.text: A nightly dump loses everything since the last dump.
Point-in-time recovery uses a base backup plus archived WAL.
You can restore to any moment, like just before a bad query.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (pg_dump, PITR, WAL) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says a nightly dump loses no data.

evidence.text: A backup you never restored may be broken or incomplete.
Regular restores prove the process and its timing before a real emergency.
After restoring, check it starts, row counts and recent data match, and the app can use it.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (restore test) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says having backup files is enough.

groups.title: Roles & Privileges
groups.question: Walk through how you would control who can see and change data in PostgreSQL.

followUps.PostgreSQL Roles & Least Privilege: Why is it risky for an application to connect as a superuser, and what should its role be allowed to do?
followUps.Row-Level Security (RLS): How does row-level security protect a multi-tenant app from a missing tenant filter in one query?

evidence.text: A superuser app account means an injection or bad migration can drop or read anything.
The app role should only have the privileges it needs, like SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE on its own tables.
Migrations and admin work use separate roles.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (roles, GRANT, least privilege) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says connecting as superuser is fine if the password is strong.

evidence.text: Row-level security attaches a policy to the table that the database applies to every query.
Even if one query forgets WHERE tenant_id, the database only returns that tenant's rows.
The tenant comes from the session (role or setting), not from each query.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (RLS, policy) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says RLS is a filter the application adds to queries.

groups.title: Security Hardening
groups.question: Explain how you would protect a database against stolen data and prove what happened after an incident.

followUps.Encryption at Rest & in Transit: What does encryption in transit protect against, what does encryption at rest protect against, and what does neither cover?
followUps.pgAudit — Audit Logging: Why would you turn on audit logging, and how do you keep it from filling the disk?

evidence.text: TLS in transit stops anyone on the network reading credentials and data.
Encryption at rest protects disks, snapshots and backups if they're stolen.
Neither protects against a valid but malicious or compromised account, or SQL injection.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (TLS, encryption at rest) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says encryption protects against every attack.

evidence.text: Audit logging records who ran what, for incidents and compliance.
Log only what you need (e.g. DDL and writes, or sensitive tables) instead of everything.
Rotate and ship logs off the server so they don't fill the disk.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (pgAudit, audit log) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says logging every statement forever has no cost.

groups.title: Monitoring & Observability
groups.question: Walk through how you keep an eye on a production database and change it safely.

followUps.pg_stat_* Views — Built-in Monitoring: Which built-in statistics views would you check first when a database gets slow, and what are you looking for?
followUps.Production Migrations — Zero-Downtime Pa: Walk through the expand and contract steps for changing a column on a busy table without downtime.

evidence.text: pg_stat_activity shows current queries, how long they've run and what they're waiting on.
pg_stat_user_tables shows sequential vs index scans and dead tuples.
pg_stat_statements shows which queries take the most total time.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (pg_stat_activity, pg_stat_statements) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says PostgreSQL has no built-in statistics views.

evidence.text: Add the new column (nullable) without blocking.
Write to both, backfill old rows in small batches, then switch reads to the new column.
Only after nothing uses the old column, drop it.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (expand/contract, migration) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says you can change the column in one ALTER on a busy table safely.
